name: Screeching Weasel
label: Lookout!
lede: Two Chicago suburbanites, four breakups and a catalog that taught a generation of pop-punk bands how to sound like the Ramones on a bad day.

eras.title: All Night Garage Sale, then a $200 debut
eras.text: Two suburban Chicago kids, Ben Weasel and Jughead, start a band and burn through bassists and drummers while cutting records on shoestring budgets. It ends in 1989 with the rhythm section off to a side project.

years.h: Prospect Heights, Illinois: [[Ben Weasel|bdce6736-8bc6-4818-8fd7-781822b674a9]] and Jughead start a band
years.p: They first play as All Night Garage Sale before settling on Screeching Weasel, with Vinnie Bovine on bass and Steve Cheese on drums.

years.h: Debut LP on Underdog, recorded in one night for $200
years.p: The self-titled first album is cut cheap and fast, with Weasel on vocals and bass and Jughead on guitar.

years.h: Boogadaboogadaboogada! on Roadkill Records
years.p: Vinnie Bovine is fired and Warren Fischer takes over bass. It is the album where the band's Ramones-and-bubblegum sound takes shape.
years.xp: Drummer Steve Cheese was also let go, reportedly for refusing to tour beyond Chicago, and [[Aaron Cometbus|47e0c017-6e9e-408b-8c9e-e01950fb4892]] filled in for two shows. Brian Vermin took the drum seat.

years.h: [[Larry Livermore|427f8569-3791-4887-976c-242bb49a573f]] sees them at Gilman Street and remembers it
years.p: Livermore of Lookout Records catches Screeching Weasel on a bill with Operation Ivy at Berkeley's 924 Gilman Street. He had earlier offered to put out a record, and was turned down.

years.h: Punkhouse EP on Limited Potential
years.p: Dan Vapid joins on bass after Fischer quits following a rough tour. The band then stops when Vapid and Vermin choose their side project Sludgeworth.

years.h: First breakup: the rhythm section picks Sludgeworth
years.p: Ben Weasel and Jughead move on to The Gore Gore Girls, and Weasel also sings briefly with the first incarnation of [[The Vindictives|553600a9-b0a7-4526-91c5-b8dcff29a895]].

eras.title: A benefit show that wouldn't stay one
eras.text: A debt-clearing reunion gig turns into a real band again, this time with Dan Panic on drums and Vapid writing with Weasel. The result, My Brain Hurts, is the record fans point to first.

years.cap: Mike Kennerty in Seattle, Washington, USA on July 1, 2006 · Wikimedia
years.h: A one-off benefit show to pay old recording debts
years.p: Ben Weasel, Jughead, Dan Vapid, Brian Vermin and Doug Ward reunite for one night. It goes well enough that the band stays together.

years.h: Ben Weasel gives up guitar; Dan Panic takes the drums
years.p: Weasel decides to concentrate on singing, and Dan Sullivan, known as Dan Panic, joins. Dave Naked plays bass for the next record.

q: We were struggling on a tour...then hundreds of people showed up.
years.src: Wikipedia: My Brain Hurts · Alternative Press: Year of the Weasel
years.h: Four days at Art of Ears: My Brain Hurts
years.p: Recorded July 2, 3, 8 and 9, 1991 in San Francisco with Andy Ernst and [[Larry Livermore|427f8569-3791-4887-976c-242bb49a573f]], and released on Lookout as LK 50.
years.xp:
Livermore said the band had every song worked out in advance, so 14 tracks plus three compilation songs went down in days. Weasel called Dan Vapid the only person he felt comfortable writing with.

A dispute nearly sank the deal: the song named above had been promised to filmmaker Bruce LaBruce. Weasel also wanted a new band name, but Livermore's contract kept the Screeching Weasel brand.

years.h: Blown tire on the way to Gilman Street goes onstage
years.p: On tour behind the Lookout signing, the band gets a flat en route to 924 Gilman Street and hauls the ruined tire on stage that night.

eras.title: Ramones, paranoia and the Lookout run
eras.text: Three Lookout albums in two years, a full Ramones cover record, and a lineup that keeps rearranging. The run ends when Ben Weasel decides he is done playing live.

years.h: A whole album of [[Ramones|d6ed7887-a401-47a8-893c-34b967444d26]] songs, on Selfless Records
years.p: Screeching Weasel covers the debut Ramones album, a tribute that says plainly where the band's sound came from.

years.h: Wiggle: first record with producer Mass Giorgini
years.p: Scott "Gub" Conway plays bass on the Lookout album and [[Mass Giorgini|abcbcb2a-f783-4300-ba85-3cb1a32c6b2b]] of Squirtgun first works with the band.

years.src: Wikipedia: Anthem for a New Tomorrow
years.h: Anthem for a New Tomorrow: a panic attack set to music
years.p: Recorded at Sonic Iguana in Lafayette, Indiana, with Dan Vapid moving to bass and Weasel on second guitar. Weasel wrote nearly everything and said he was chasing the feel of a panic attack.
years.xp: Weasel has cited Wire's Pink Flag as a template. Vapid co-wrote only the song "Trance." Later musicians including Dustin Kensrue of Thrice and Mark Rubano of Taking Back Sunday have praised its mix of playful and dark.

years.h: How to Make Enemies and Irritate People closes the Lookout era
years.p: The last album of the run, made just before Ben Weasel called it quits again.

years.big: Done with the stage, done with Dan
years.h: Second breakup: Weasel stops wanting to play live
years.p: Ben Weasel no longer wants to perform, and Dan Vapid leaves after a falling out with him. Weasel, Vapid and Dan Panic form The Riverdales, which tour with Green Day.
years.xp: The breakup ended the Lookout run of My Brain Hurts, Wiggle, Anthem and How to Make Enemies. The Riverdales kept the pop-punk sound going with the same three players.

eras.title: Fat Wreck years and the third breakup
eras.text: The band returns with Mass Giorgini on bass and a new Squirtgun rhythm section, records for Fat Wreck Chords and its own Panic Button imprint, and splits again over touring.

years.h: Bark Like a Dog: back on Fat Wreck Chords
years.p: Ben Weasel and Jughead return with Mass Giorgini and Dan Lumley of Squirtgun and guitarist Zac Damon. Dan Vapid and Dan Panic play on the record but then step aside by mutual decision.

years.h: Bark Like a Dog reaches No. 34 on Billboard Heatseekers
years.p: Wikipedia lists it as their highest-charting album.

years.h: Ben Weasel and Jughead found Panic Button Records
years.p: The band's own label releases the Major Label Debut EP, while Television City Dream comes out on Fat Wreck Chords.

years.h: Television City Dream on Fat Wreck Chords
years.p: Their second album for Mike Burkett's label, with Zac Damon, Mass Giorgini and Dan Lumley.

years.h: Emo on Panic Button, recorded without Zac Damon
years.p: Damon sits it out for school, and the band continues as a four-piece.

years.h: Teen Punks in Heat, the last record of the third run
years.p: Around this time they play their first live shows since 1993, 30-minute matinees at Chicago's House of Blues.

years.h: Third breakup: Jughead wants to tour and Weasel doesn't
years.p: Jughead is frustrated at the lack of touring, and the band ends on July 6, 2001.

eras.title: Solo books, a lawsuit-shaped silence and two one-offs
eras.text: The band is dormant, but its catalog is not: Ben Weasel takes the masters back from Lookout and Asian Man reissues them.

years.h: Ben Weasel publishes a novel, Like Hell, and a solo LP
years.p: He releases Fidatevi and writes a fictional punk-band novel, while Jughead forms Even in Blackouts and later writes Weasels in a Box.

years.h: Weasel takes the Screeching Weasel masters back from Lookout!
years.p: After a long fight over money, the catalog is relicensed and reissued via Asian Man Records; Lookout's royalties dispute is the stated cause per Wikipedia. The band plays surprise sets at Chicago's Fireside Bowl.
years.xp: Wikipedia says Weasel left Lookout in 2005 over unpaid royalties, giving different years for the same split, which is why this card holds both facts.

years.h: Weasel and Vapid play My Brain Hurts in full at Reggie's Rock Club
years.p: Two Chicago shows for the anniversary.

eras.title: Without Jughead, and the SXSW night
eras.text: Ben Weasel restarts the band without his co-founder after a legal fight, releases First World Manifesto, then blows it up at SXSW.

years.h: Weasel reforms Screeching Weasel without Jughead
years.p: Ben Weasel announces the reunion on his blog, citing legal issues that stopped him from having his own band. Jughead posts a long MySpace statement saying the band was never supposed to exist without both of them.
years.xp: Weasel described the split as the result of a two-year legal fight over band business rather than an amicable parting, and later moved catalog work from Asian Man to Recess Records. The new lineup was Weasel, Dan Vapid, guitarist Simon Lamb or Drew Fredrichsen, bassist Justin Perkins and drummer Adam Cargin.

years.h: First World Manifesto, the first album in eleven years
years.p: Fat Wreck Chords releases the record, produced by Mike Kennerty of The All-American Rejects.

years.h: SXSW at Scoot Inn: Weasel punches an audience member, four bandmates quit
years.p: According to Wikipedia, Weasel punched a woman who had thrown beer and ice and spat on him; he apologized March 22, and four members resigned March 23 via Punknews.org.
years.xp: Fat Mike said in July 2011 he had no interest in releasing another Screeching Weasel record.

eras.title: Never breaking up again
eras.text: A new lineup at Reggie's, crowd-funded rock opera, a run of records, and sold-out Chicago shows in 2025.

years.h: Back at Reggie's Rock Club with The Queers
years.p: Ben Weasel returns with Zac Damon, Dave Klein, Pierre Marche and Mike Hunchback, then releases the Carnival of Schadenfreude EP on Recess in November.

years.h: Crowd-funded rock opera Baby Fat: Act 1
years.p: Announced by Weasel on YouTube in July 2014, it raises over $40,000.

years.h: Some Freaks of Atavism on Monona Music
years.p: The 13th studio album, followed by The Awful Disclosures of Screeching Weasel in July 2022, produced by Mike Kennerty, who also joins on guitar.

years.h: Chicago shows sell out in under an hour
years.p: After the pandemic pause, Screeching Weasel announces live dates. Weasel's stated line: the band never breaks up again and dies when he does.
